frontmatter.title: Eye Gaze and Mouse Movement Synchronization

children.value: Gaze was recorded by the EyeLink on its own clock, the cursor by the task on the task clock. This chapter describes how both are put on one clock per trial, how precise the alignment is, and the measures computed from the synchronised streams. The results are in

The 87 participants with usable eye-tracking data all have a cursor file: 15,177 usable trials with 97,778 tokens (net placements; None 32, Partial 35, Full Instructions 20 participants).
The task writes a cursor sample on every frame it polls (every 33–50 ms), with
in task units (degrees of visual angle; the slots lie at radius 8), the phase (anticipation, placement, ISI) and the button state. The cursor is not recorded during the outcome. Within a trial,
is constant (SD 0.004 ms), so both columns share one clock.

The task writes the first cursor sample of a phase at the first frame of that phase, and sends the phase message at the same point. For every trial, the time stamp of the first placement sample (task clock) is paired with
of the same trial (EDF clock), and a straight line
is fitted per participant. Pairs more than 20 ms off the first line are left out and the line is refitted (2 of 15,636 pairs in all). Every cursor sample is mapped to the EDF clock with this line.

The two clocks run at slightly different rates (60 ppm). Over a session of about 55 minutes this adds up to about 0.2 s, so a single offset would not be enough; the linear fit removes it.
After the fit, placement onsets agree within about ±1.5 ms; the time resolution of the cursor (33–50 ms per sample) is far coarser than this.

The anticipation and ISI onsets, which are not used for the fit, agree within ±1 ms around a constant −10 ms: relative to the placement anchor, the first sample of these phases is written about 10 ms before the message is sent. This constant does not change the alignment within the placement phase, which all eye–hand measures use; for the anticipation phase the cursor times are therefore accurate to about 10 ms.

Gaze bins with at least half of the 1000 Hz samples valid are converted to degrees from the screen centre (33.7 px per degree, y upwards, as the cursor) and corrected with the drift offset of the trial’s block. Their time is the centre of the 20 ms bin. The gaze entropy here is computed from the 20 ms gaze stream in the same way as the cursor entropy, so the two are directly comparable; the fixation-based gaze entropy of the eye-tracking analysis (over task locations or slots, fixations only) is reported alongside.
